extracted.intended_audience: British public and policymakers sympathetic to conservative critique of the French Revolution (late 18th-century readers)
extracted.subtask_description: A late-18th-century conservative pamphlet arguing against the French Revolution and radical philosophic reforms, defending established institutions, manners, religion, and gradual justice. It aims to persuade the educated public and policymakers to resist revolutionary change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reprobation of triumphing in regicide or sacrilege
rubrics_metrics.description: One ought not to rejoice or celebrate the murder of kings, queens, bishops, or infants; such exultation is shocking except to those 'made for accomplishing revolutions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke reproves the 'burst of enthusiasm' that treats the fall or murder of high personages as a 'beautiful day' or precursor of Millennium; he stresses humane sensibility toward victims and condemns rhetorical sketches that would finish such massacres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensibility to rank, sex, beauty, and youth as moral guides
rubrics_metrics.description: The exalted rank, sex, beauty, amiable qualities, and tender age of sufferers ought to increase our sensibility rather than prompt exultation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke explains that natural human feelings—pity for the innocent and admiration for virtue—teach moral lessons and should temper political judgment; these feelings are proper and not mere sentimentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of celebrating political crimes for contingent advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: It is dangerous to weigh actual crime against contingent advantage and to justify perfidy or murder in the ledger of 'public benefit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theatre-analogy: audiences reject Machiavellian calculations that post crimes against advantages; tolerating criminal means for public ends leads to preference for crime and erosion of moral restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law must be supported by affections and manners, not terrors alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws cannot be sustained solely by fear or private interest; public affections and manners are required as supplements, correctives, and aids to law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted maxim: 'Non satis est pulchra esse poemata, dulcia sunto.' Burke argues that institutions need to be embodied in persons and loved, not merely mechanically enforced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the 'system of manners' that makes a nation lovely
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-formed nation's manners and moral imagination are necessary to make the country lovable and to engender attachment and loyalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns that discarding the 'decent drapery of life' and the 'superadded ideas' from moral imagination will destroy those social affections which soften and beautify politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value chivalry and the spirit of gentlemanly honor
rubrics_metrics.description: The ancient chivalrous spirit produced noble equality, mitigated pride and power, and cultivated social esteem, elegance, and honorable behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loss of this spirit ('the age of chivalry is gone') means losing generosity, dignified obedience, and the 'nurse of manly sentiment and heroic enterprise', with broad cultural decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain religion as the basis of civil society
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion is the foundation of civil society, the source of all good and comfort; a nation should not call in impiety to reform religion or institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke contends that most people prefer piety to impiety; churches and religious establishments supply the moral supports that sustain learning, manners, and commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve established institutions in their existing degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: One should keep 'an established church, an established monarchy, an established aristocracy, and an established democracy, each in the degree it exists, and in no greater.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit conservative program: resist dismantling or wholesale reengineering of historically rooted institutions; reforms should not exceed their traditional scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect tradition and prejudice as practical moral capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Longstanding prejudices and customs can embody latent wisdom and are useful because they make virtue habitual and give ready motives in emergencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues prejudice, combined with embedded reasons, provides steadiness of conduct and prevents paralysis of private reason in moments of decision; do not discard prejudices merely because they are old.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against mechanistic philosophy that banishes affections
rubrics_metrics.description: Cold, mechanistic reason that excludes affections undermines the moral foundations of society and cannot supply the replacements lost when sentiment and manners are excised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke portrays a 'mechanic philosophy' whose groves present nothing but gallows; such reason reduces human attachments and thus fails to create love, veneration, or attachment to institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid revolutionary experiments that destroy commerce and arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Commerce, trade, and manufactures grew under the protection of manners and religion; experiments that remove these protections risk destroying commerce and the arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns that when protecting principles are lost, trade and manufacture may decay and a nation may become poor, brutish, and devoid of honor or religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge a nation by a noisy minority
rubrics_metrics.description: A few vocal cabals or noisy agitators do not represent the general dispositions of a nation; avoid generalizing from a small faction to the whole people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The metaphor: half a dozen grasshoppers make the field ring while thousands of cattle are silent; beware forming policy based on the clamour of small groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punish tyrants with grave, decorous justice, not spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: The punishment of real tyrants may be just, but justice should be grave and decorous—dignified vengeance differs from triumphant insult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke contrasts venal triumph with solemn justice; even when punishing wicked rulers, act in a manner befitting justice rather than indecorous celebration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise prudence before degrading or trusting deposed rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: It is inconsistent and imprudent to degrade a man publicly as the worst criminal and then entrust him with high offices; decisions about leaders should be coherent with prior condemnations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointments that both insult and then rely on the same person imply a breach of trust and political inconsistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust respect for magistrates, parliaments, and the social hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Society depends on respect toward kings, parliaments, magistrates, priests, and nobility; such deference is 'natural' and supports rational liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke asserts that English people inwardly feel reverence and that abandoning these affections leads to corruption of primary morals and readiness for servitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of philosophic cabals organized to overturn institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophic or 'freethinker' cabals acting in corps to influence public affairs are dangerous when they displace the traditional sources of authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke notes that in England such writers existed but were unconnected individuals who did not form a faction; organized philosophical factions threaten constitutional stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain guardianship structures that support learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning survived under the protection of nobility and clergy; preserving their roles helps keep learning alive and prevents its degradation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns that detaching learning from its traditional protectors will cast it 'into the mire' and that patrons and institutions are integral to cultural continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose reducing persons to mere animals or economic units
rubrics_metrics.description: Political theories that demote kings, queens, or women to 'merely animals' or treat human relations as transactional are corrosive of honour and social goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke criticizes philosophies that strip the 'decent drapery of life' and regard homages to sex or rank as mere romance and folly, leading to moral coarseness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject governance-as-fashion thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: The view that government may change like fashions ('modes of dress') is misguided; constitutions require durable attachments, not ephemeral convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke faults 'new statesmen' who treat constitutions as interchangeable with momentary projects; attachment should be deeper than present utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defend national character and slow, cautious reform
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation's historical character and gradual habits matter; rash imitation of foreign models (e.g., French revolutionary methods) risks national ruin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke counsels that foreign experiments should be kept at a distance—if they are a panacea we don't want it; if a plague, quarantine is required. He predicts disasters for imitators.
